title: Learning Lesson 5: We Forget Stuff
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: This lesson closes out Stephen Chew's four learning "bottlenecks" with the last one: we forget stuff, a limitation Stuart insists applies to every human being, not just struggling students. He grounds the abstract idea in relatable examples — forgetting a former classmate's name, forgetting a parent's birthday, blanking on a math problem you "know" you learned — to normalize forgetting before offering the fix. The solution combines two elements: overlearning (already introduced as the fix for the concentration bottleneck) and distinctiveness, which Stuart illustrates via Chew's example of confusable versus non-confusable lists (ice cream flavors versus sundaes and sushi). The lesson ends by having students recite all four bottlenecks and their paired solutions from memory, reinforcing the retrieval-practice approach the series itself models.
points: Forgetting is framed as a universal cognitive limitation, not a personal failing, using everyday examples (forgotten names, forgotten birthdays, blanked-on test answers) to normalize it before teaching the fix.

The solution to forgetting reuses the overlearning concept from the concentration lesson and adds a second ingredient: distinctiveness, meaning material that isn't easily confused with similar material.

Chew's food-list example (sundae/sushi versus sundae/banana split/malt) makes the abstract idea of "distinctiveness" concrete by showing how easily confusable items are harder to remember than clearly distinct ones.
The lesson closes the four-bottleneck arc with a cumulative recall check, having students retrieve all four bottlenecks and solutions from memory rather than simply rereading them.
quotes: You're walking down the hallway and see that classmate from seventh grade, but you can't remember their name. Your mom's birthday comes and goes and you don't say anything. (Never do this!!!)
So the solution here is going to look familiar: overlearned, distinctive memories resist forgetting.
He says that these lists are distinct; they are non-confusable. You're not going to mix up sundaes and sushi. But what if it was a list of different kinds of ice cream desserts?
That overlearning part should look familiar — it's the solution to concentration being hard, too. But the distinctive part is new.
We forget stuff — so overlearn things and think hard about their distinctive meanings.
